title: The tomb in Shiraz
hookLine: people gather at Hafiz's tomb to recite his poems
tomorrow: Zoe writes her own ghazal for tonight. where does her name go?

lines: WHAT DO YOU EVEN DO THERE?
cards: Inés is going to her grandmother's grave for the first time since the burial, and she's asked Zoe to come. In the car she says it plainly: I don't know what you even do there.
Yesterday's question had an answer waiting in Shiraz. People go to Hafiz's grave, and they read him his own poems.

teach.h: A PLACE OF PILGRIMAGE, HE SAID.
teach.b: Hafiz saw it coming. In one ghazal he writes: when you pass by my grave, ask for a blessing, for it will become a place of pilgrimage for the free spirits of the world.

teach.h: THE HAFEZIEH: POEMS AT THE STONE.
teach.b: Today his tomb stands in a garden in Shiraz, the Hafezieh. Visitors recite his ghazals there, some open the Divan for a line, some just sit with a hand on the stone. Under that custom sits a teaching.
In Islam, visiting a grave is called ziyarat. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says he had once forbidden visiting graves, but now: visit them.

teach.h: ZIYARAT: THEY REMIND YOU OF DEATH.
teach.b: Another hadith there gives the reason: they remind you of death. Hadiths in the same book teach a greeting of peace for the dead, and the Prophet asking forgiveness for them.
The question for this week: why go back to a grave at all? Inés's own tradition answers too.
The Catholic Bible says, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins."
Shared: you go back, and you bring words to the one you lost; both traditions pray for the dead.
Honestly different: Catholics pray for the soul, trusting that prayer helps it on its way to God. At the Hafezieh, people also bring the poet his own words, the way he asked.
Two ways of standing at a grave, neither one a copy of the other.

how: Visitors to the Hafezieh in Shiraz recite Hafiz's ghazals and open his Divan at the tomb. In Islam, ziyarat (visiting graves) includes greeting the dead with peace; Catholics visit graves and pray for the dead.

games.q: what does “the tomb in shiraz” mean?
o: Hafiz's grave, where visitors recite his poems
a royal tomb where Persian kings are buried
the mosque in Shiraz where Hafiz taught

games.q: two ways of standing at a grave: tap the pairs.
p: a holy thought to pray for the dead
what Hafiz asks of those passing his grave

s: Hafiz wrote that his grave would draw pilgrims
a ghazal says his tomb will become a place of pilgrimage for the free spirits of the world.
in Islam, visiting graves is forbidden
in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says: visit them, for they remind you of death.
Catholics at a grave and visitors at Hafiz's tomb do exactly the same thing
both bring words back to the dead, and both pray for them, in their own ways. at Hafiz's tomb, people also recite the poet's own lines.

games.q: your friend's grandmother was Catholic; your friend isn't sure what she believes anymore. at the grave she asks, 'what do I even say?' what fits today?
o: say her words: a prayer she loved, or a line she lived by.
say nothing; words at a grave are only for believers.
don't stay long; a grave visit just makes grief last longer.
games.why: in Shiraz, people recite the poet's own lines at his tomb; Catholics pray for the dead. either way, words come back to the grave.

practice: Bring to mind one grave or memorial you know, or one person you've lost. Count three things they gave you, slowly, one for each long breath.
If you pray, you can pray for them in the words of your own tradition; if not, simply hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: The tomb in Shiraz: Hafiz's grave in a garden, where visitors recite his poems, just as one of his ghazals foresaw.

orig.note: Arabic and Persian: a visit, especially to a grave or a shrine.

carryVoice: Your line: reciting at the tomb, bringing their own words back to them. Seven days into Hafiz.
